risks.note: Energy accounts for 30-40% of cement production cost. Volatile coal, petcoke, diesel and electricity prices, supply disruptions and dependence on imports directly compress margins when price pass through is limited - and higher power, fuel and logistics costs were the stated cause of the Q4 FY26 profit decline.

Cement is a highly competitive and regionally fragmented market due to high transportation costs. Price wars, discounting and an inability to sustain price hikes bite hardest when new capacities are added faster than demand growth; pricing pressure in the Gujarat cement market weighed on FY26 profitability.

Demand is tied to construction, infrastructure, housing and economic cycles. Economic slowdown, delayed government projects, real estate downturns, seasonal monsoons and uneven regional demand are flagged, and excess industry capacity can further pressure prices and profitability.

Production depends heavily on limestone, coal/petcoke, gypsum and fly ash. Limited limestone reserves, mining approvals, variability in raw material quality and dependence on industrial by-products such as fly ash - whose availability depends on thermal power plants - can raise costs or halt production.

risks.risk: Environmental and regulatory risk, including carbon
risks.note: Cement manufacturing is highly polluting and carbon intensive, facing strict regulation on CO2 emissions, dust, NOx, water usage and mining rehabilitation. Tighter norms, carbon pricing, compliance costs and litigation may require heavy capex for pollution control or carbon reduction technologies. The BRSR material-issues table separately flags regulatory compliance in a dynamic regulatory landscape as a risk with negative financial implications.

Cement plants require large upfront capital investment; risks include high debt levels, interest rate fluctuations, refinancing risk, liquidity constraints and lower than expected returns if demand weakens or costs rise, with over-expansion during upcycles often leading to stress during downturns. Interest expense rose sharply in FY26 on the capacity expansion effective 1 October 2025.

Cement has a low value to weight ratio, making logistics critical. High freight costs, fuel price escalation, port bottlenecks, rail shortages, trucking disruptions and regional supply imbalances reduce competitiveness in distant markets.

The CODM has identified one business segment - manufacturing and sale of cement - with the Company's only production facility located in India and no other reportable segments; BRSR shows exports contributing just 0.20% of total turnover, so earnings hinge on one product, one plant and essentially one domestic market.

one-line thesis: Shree Digvijay has executed a strategic Brand Usage & Distribution Agreement (BDA) with Hi-Bond Cement, instantly scaling combined capacity to 5.2 MTPA and securing ~10% Gujarat market share without immediate capex burden. While Q4FY26 benefits from a INR 25-30/bag price hike and stable costs, FY27 margins face a structural ~INR 200/ton compression due to increased reliance on purchased clinker to feed new grinding capacity, partially offset by high-margin oil well cement (15% of revenue).
financial scorecard: Revenue: Guided up 8-10% YoY in Q4 on volume + price; EBITDA/margin: Q4 stable, but FY27 EBITDA/ton expected to dip ~INR 200 due to clinker outsourcing; PAT: Not disclosed, linked to volume ramp; Order book: N/A (commodity); Net debt: Rose to INR 485 Cr (INR 132 Cr existing + INR 356 Cr new loan for BDA), interest rate 8.7%.
guidance: Revenue growth: 8-10% YoY in Q4; double-digit volume growth expected FY27; Margin: Q4 stable, FY27 pressure from clinker costs offset by product mix; Order inflow: N/A; Capex/commissioning: 1.5 MTPA grinding unit commissioned Oct 2025, no new capex planned until 70-75% utilization reached.
order book & pipeline: N/A - Commodity business; Sales volume guided at 3.0-3.5 MTPA for FY27 (combined entity).
segment / subsidiary detail: Core Cement (OPC/PPC/Slag): 85% of volume, focused on Saurashtra/Gujarat; Oil Well Cement: 7-8% volume but 15% revenue contribution, 90% market share in India among oil well players; Hi-Bond Integration: Adds 2.2 MTPA grinding capacity, currently operating at ~1 MTPA.
growth verticals / optionality: Market share expansion in Gujarat from 10% to 14-15%; Potential exercise of call option on Hi-Bond assets post-milestone alignment; Captive jetty commercialization (discussions with Reliance/TPS for 1-1.5 MTPA cargo, not yet confirmed); Limestone mine acquisitions (20 MTPA recently acquired, 600 MTPA reserve in vicinity).
margins & cost dynamics: Q4FY26: Net price increase INR 25-30/bag, no cost inflation expected; FY27 Outlook: EBITDA/ton compression of ~INR 200 due to purchased clinker (clinker factor ~55%); Hi-Bond contribution: Expected INR 200-300/ton EBITDA after paying cost-plus-INR 500 fee; Fuel risk: Brent crude/petcoke rise to be passed through to customers.
capex / expansion: Recent: 1.5 MTPA grinding unit commissioned Oct 2025; Future: No immediate clinkerization capex; Plan to explore limestone mines and potential clinker plant only after reaching 70-75% utilization of current 5.2 MTPA capacity.
capital allocation: Debt-funded growth: INR 356 Cr raised for BDA transaction; Deleveraging: Repaying INR 24-25 Cr annually; Promoter stance: Long-term view by IRF (Piramal/Bain), professional management run.
risks & watch-items: Margin dilution from high clinker procurement costs; Geopolitical supply chain disruptions affecting clinker/coal imports; Delay in commercializing captive jetty; Execution risk in integrating Hi-Bond operations; Dependence on Gujarat/Saurashtra regional demand.
management quality / tone: Cautiously optimistic; Emphasizes volume growth over immediate margin expansion; Transparent about clinker cost headwinds but confident in pass-through mechanisms; Professional and process-driven regarding potential Hi-Bond acquisition.
non-obvious takeaways: Oil Well Cement division commands ~90% share of Indian oil well cement market (ONGC, Oil India, Schlumberger) contributing disproportionately to revenue (15%) vs volume (7-8%); Hi-Bond plant has captive power meeting 80% needs, making its base production cost lower than Digvijay's, creating an arbitrage even after the INR 500/ton fee.

themes.title: Cement demand & pricing recovery
themes.need: Q1FY27 turned cement from a pricing story into a volume-share-plus-fuel-cost story. ULTRACEMCO grew domestic grey volume +13.1% YoY against an estimated ~7-8% industry, delivered its first Rs 5,000cr+ April-June EBITDA (Rs 5,146cr) with EBITDA/ton held above Rs 1,200, and crossed 200.1 MT domestic capacity a year early - but guided Q2FY27 cost UP ~Rs 130-140/ton and pinned the Rs 1,400/ton consolidated target to Q4FY28. The fuel shock, not price, is the swing factor: JKCEMENT's EBITDA/ton fell to Rs 982 from Rs 1,229 YoY despite +19% grey volume, DALBHARAT flagged pet coke 'surged to nearly $160/t' versus a pre-war $110-115, and NUVOCO defended INR 1,079/ton EBITDA only by cutting petcoke from 37% to 27% of fuel mix in a single quarter. Consolidation is visibly compounding (INDIACEM EBITDA/ton Rs 386->400->509->603 across four quarters; DALBHARAT closed Jaypee at Rs 2,850cr EV with Chunar operational and Rewa on trial within 50 days) even as DALBHARAT slipped its 75mt milestone from FY27 to FY28. SHREECEM/RAMCOCEM/JKLAKSHMI/JSWCEMENT/STARCEMENT/BIRLACORPN ride the same volume + consolidation axis.
themes.driver: Q2FY27 is the guided cost trough - ULTRACEMCO ~Rs 130-140/ton, JKCEMENT ~Rs 150/ton and BIRLACORPN Rs 70-80/ton of incremental cost; then fuel-mix agility (NUVOCO's petcoke swing) and whether DALBHARAT's ~Rs 150/t of procurement savings is really 'permanent, not timing'.

demand_drivers.title: Demand & outlook drivers
demand_drivers.body:
- Indian cement demand expected to grow by about 6-7% annually in the near term, broadly in line with India's GDP growth, supported by infrastructure development, housing, urbanisation and government capital expenditure.
- India's cement demand projected to increase 7-8% in FY26, driven primarily by government housing initiatives like the Pradhan Mantri Awas Yojana and ongoing infrastructure development projects.
- The GST revamp announced in September 2025 is expected to reduce cement prices by Rs 30-35 per 50-kg bag, lowering construction costs and potentially stimulating demand.
- Gujarat-specific demand catalysts: the Mumbai-Ahmedabad Bullet Train Corridor using around 20,000 cubic meters of cement daily, and the 2030 Commonwealth Games in Gujarat driving real estate and infrastructure upgrades in Ahmedabad, Gandhinagar and Rajkot.
- Cement plants near the ports, for instance the plants in Gujarat, are seen as having an added advantage for export and being better placed logistically than plants in the interior.
- Increasing industry consolidation and rising capacity utilisation have improved pricing discipline and operational efficiency, although competitive intensity remains high.
- Cost pressures from fuel, freight and currency movements persist; management attributes the FY26 profit decline to extremely poor cement prices plus higher interest expense from the capacity expansion, and the Q4 FY26 profit fall to higher power, fuel and logistics costs and pricing pressure in the Gujarat cement market.
- Operating efficiency lever: EBITDA per tonne rose to around Rs 521 from Rs 489, on better cost control and improved realizations especially during the later part of the year.
- Green and low carbon cement flagged as a key long term opportunity under India's Net Zero 2070 commitment, encouraging blended cements, alternative fuels, waste heat recovery and carbon reduction technologies.
- Sector profitability backdrop cited from ICRA: India's cement sector operating profit expected to rise 12-18% to Rs 900-950 per metric tonne in FY26.

Alongside this brownfield addition, a 10 year strategic tie up with Hi Bond Cement adds 2.2 MTPA of asset light capacity, taking effective capacity to about 5.2 MTPA; management frames this as strengthening market share and revenue visibility while offering a future acquisition option, and as a strategic shift from manufacturing led growth to a distribution driven model selling both 'Kamal Cement' and 'Hi-Bond Cement'. The expansion carried a financing cost: the Directors' Report attributes higher interest expense during the year to the capacity expansion that became effective on October 01, 2025. moat.title: Bull — competitive strengths
moat.body:
- Own limestone mining, described as a key operational activity sourcing the primary raw material - fully mechanized, carried out without drilling and blasting, with a multi-pit approach blending low-grade and high-grade limestone for optimal mineral utilisation
- Green power depth: Waste Heat Recovery System plus wind and hybrid power under PPAs supplied 48.39% of total electricity consumption in FY 2025-26, a structural cost and emissions advantage
- Blended-cement mix of 49.30% of output, continuing to reduce the average clinker factor across the portfolio
- Zero Liquid Discharge facility with 100% of industrial water recycled and specific water intensity cut from 0.138 KL/t cement to 0.045 KL/t cement
- Capacity doubled to 3.0 Million Tons per annum from 1st October 2025, adding scale at an established site

- Digital transformation embedded across sales, logistics, materials management, manufacturing and control systems

risks.title: Risks & watch-items
risks.body: Margin dilution from high clinker procurement costs; Geopolitical supply chain disruptions affecting clinker/coal imports; Delay in commercializing captive jetty; Execution risk in integrating Hi-Bond operations; Dependence on Gujarat/Saurashtra regional demand.

non_obvious.title: Non-obvious takeaways
non_obvious.body: Oil Well Cement division commands ~90% share of Indian oil well cement market (ONGC, Oil India, Schlumberger) contributing disproportionately to revenue (15%) vs volume (7-8%); Hi-Bond plant has captive power meeting 80% needs, making its base production cost lower than Digvijay's, creating an arbitrage even after the INR 500/ton fee.

strategy.title: Strategies (RHP)
strategy.body:
- Scale up manufacturing at Sikka: the new grinding unit commissioned in October 2025 doubled capacity to 3.0 MTPA, enhancing scale and competitiveness in Gujarat.
- Asset light capacity addition through a 10 year strategic tie up with Hi Bond Cement that adds 2.2 MTPA, taking effective capacity to about 5.2 MTPA and offering a future acquisition option.
- Shift from a manufacturing led growth model to a distribution driven model, with an exclusive long-term arrangement to distribute 100% of the cement products manufactured and supplied by Hi-Bond.
- Multi brand strategy - selling both 'Kamal Cement' …
